Assistant: [Acknowledges]

User: Oh and that Vercel blog post about partial prerendering was really helpful for understanding the migration: https://vercel.com/blog/partial-prerendering

Assistant: [Continues working]

evals.expected_output: Should tier findings rather than emit a flat count. Worth saving: (1) feedback — Next.js 14 config goes through the `experimental` key, not raw webpack overrides; (2) feedback — components use arrow functions with explicit return types per team style guide; (3) project — App Router migration from Pages Router by end of Q2, led by Sarah on the platform team. Success is correct tiering and justification, NOT hitting a number: presenting all five as equally recommended saves is explicitly not ideal. Should present under Worth-saving and Borderline tiers, grouped by type, with proposed filenames and content previews, and ask which to save.

evals.prompt:
You are Claude in a conversation with a user. The conversation history below represents what has already happened in this session. Your task is to use the session-harvest skill to review the conversation and present findings.

---
CONVERSATION HISTORY:

User: I'm a senior iOS engineer, mostly Swift and SwiftUI. Just started learning the backend stuff for our team's new microservice.

Assistant: [Helps set up a Go project]

User: The tests keep failing with 'connection refused'. I've been staring at this for an hour.

Assistant: [Suggests checking if Docker is running, tries various network fixes]

User: Ugh none of that worked.

Assistant: [Tries more debugging approaches]

User: Wait — I just realized the issue. The test database URL was pointing to localhost but our docker-compose maps it to 'db' as the hostname. Once I changed TEST_DATABASE_URL to use 'db' instead of 'localhost', everything passed.

Assistant: [Acknowledges the fix]

User: Yeah, the lesson here is: when tests fail with connection errors in a dockerized setup, always check if the hostname matches the docker-compose service name. Don't waste time on network configuration.

Assistant: [Acknowledges]

User: Also, for future reference, our team wiki for the backend is at notion.so/acme/backend-eng. All the Docker setup docs are there.

Assistant: [Continues working]

User: Before I go, I want to make sure we remember the important stuff from today.

---

Use the session-harvest skill to analyze this conversation and present your findings. Note: for this test, you don't need to actually read/write memory files — just present what you would propose saving.
evals.expected_output: Should surface three durable items in the Worth-saving tier: (1) user — senior iOS engineer mostly in Swift/SwiftUI, newly learning backend/Go; (2) feedback/lesson — in a dockerized setup, connection-refused test failures usually mean the hostname must match the docker-compose service name, not a network-config problem; (3) reference — the team backend wiki (notion.so/acme/backend-eng) as the standing home for Docker setup docs. The team wiki is durable, reusable infrastructure, so it belongs in Worth saving, not Borderline. Should NOT memorialize the individual failed debugging steps — only the distilled lesson. Grade on value-justification and correct tiering, not on hitting the number three; items grouped by type under the Worth-saving tier with proper filenames and content previews.

evals.prompt:
You are Claude in a conversation with a user. The conversation history below represents what has already happened in this session. Your task is to use the session-harvest skill to review the conversation, present findings, and (when the user approves) write the memories — including the pre-save accuracy audit described in the skill.

---
CONVERSATION HISTORY:

User: We're debugging why our React component re-renders so often. The state update is in a useEffect.

Assistant: [Reads the component, identifies that the useEffect dependency array includes an inline object literal, which is a new reference each render]

User: Oh yeah that's it. The lesson: in React, useEffect runs every render if the dependency array contains an object literal, because object identity changes each render. We've hit this three times this month.

Assistant: [Acknowledges and fixes by lifting the object out]

User: Also I just learned that the useMemo hook was added in React 17 — before that we had to use useCallback for everything. Good to know.

Assistant: [Continues working]

User: Before I close this, harvest learnings.

---

Use the session-harvest skill. Run all phases including the accuracy audit. The user will approve all proposed items. For this test, assume your memory directory is empty (no existing memories). For verification of factual claims about React, use what you know — what matters is that the audit happens before saving.
evals.expected_output: Should propose two memories: (1) feedback about useEffect deps + object literals, and (2) something about useMemo / React 17. After the user approves both, the Phase 5 audit should catch that the second item is wrong — useMemo (and the rest of the hook API) was introduced in React 16.8 (Feb 2019), not React 17. The skill must either correct that memory before saving or drop the false claim, AND tell the user what changed before writing. A passing run does NOT silently save the wrong claim. A failing run saves both memories without flagging the React 17 error.

evals.expected_output: This is the adversarial discernment test: many moments superficially match the categories, but almost all are low-value. The Worth-saving tier should contain exactly ONE item — the feedback (or project) rule that deploys are held until Monday because the on-call rotation hands off Friday afternoon (capture both the rule and the reason). The casual sign-offs ('perfect, ship it', 'great, thanks') must NOT become feedback memories. The typo fix and the '.next/ cache' build fix are ephemeral and must be dropped, not saved. The StackOverflow link helped once and is at most a Borderline — optional reference, never a recommended save. A passing run surfaces ~1 recommended save and tiers or drops the rest; a failing run surfaces 4–5 confident saves by treating the casual approvals, the one-off fix, and the link as memory-worthy.
